statement: rules/rules.json's 20 SEC-2.* rows do NOT all carry the literal validator string "generic-scanner" the arc-10 workpack text implies ("SEC-2 (20, validator: generic-scanner)"). The actual split is: 17 rows are "generic-scanner" (SEC-2.1..2.14, 2.19, 2.2, 2.20, 2.3..2.9 minus the three below), 1 row (SEC-2.15) is "generic-scanner-redaction", and 3 rows (SEC-2.16/.17/.18) are "common/security". All 20 are still simple content-line-scan rules with the identical Validator shape, so this crate treats them as one data-driven family rather than splitting into three separate modules by validator-name string.
why: A worker trusting the workpack's summary table ("SEC-2, validator: generic-scanner") at face value and grepping rules.json for validator=="generic-scanner" would only find 17 of the 20 rows and could plausibly conclude 3 rules (SEC-2.15/.16/.17/.18) belong to some other crate/owner, when in fact all 22 SEC-* rows including these belong to arc-10 per the workpack's own family:security ownership statement.
howToApply: When a workpack table names a single validator string for a rule range, verify against rules/rules.json directly (grep by family/id, not by the named validator string) before assuming every row in that range shares that exact validator field — count by id/family, treat the validator name column as approximate/illustrative.

evidence.ref: rules/rules.json SEC-2.* validator field distribution: 17x generic-scanner, 1x generic-scanner-redaction (SEC-2.15), 3x common/security (SEC-2.16/.17/.18) — all family:security

statement: Several SEC-2 rules port a JS-source `condition && !markerPresent(line)` shape (e.g. SEC-2.11/.12/.14: real-looking secret UNLESS the line also carries an allowed placeholder marker like `example`/`fake`/`<TOKEN>`; SEC-2.16/.17/.18: a bare tool invocation UNLESS it also carries a required flag like `--sarif`/`--json`). Rust's `regex` crate (unlike JS RegExp with lookahead, or unlike a hand-rolled `!re.test(line)` check) has no negative lookaround, so a single regex cannot express "matches X but not Y" directly.
why: A worker porting these JS `&&` conditions naively into one Rust regex per rule would either fail to compile (attempting `(?!...)` syntax the `regex` crate rejects) or silently produce a wrong pattern that either always fires or never fires depending on how the negation was worked around.
howToApply: Model the JS `condition && !markerPresent(line)` shape as TWO separate compiled patterns on the `RuleSpec`: a positive `pattern` (the base violation shape) and an optional `suppressed_by_any_of: Option<Regex>` (the marker whose presence on the SAME line suppresses an otherwise-matching hit). See crates/enforcer-lang-security/src/rules/spec.rs's `RuleSpec::suppressed_by_any_of` field and `validate_content`'s `suppressed` check — this is the general two-regex equivalent of a JS `&&` negation and should be reused by any future text-scan validator crate that ports a similar JS `!re.test(...)` condition.

evidence.ref: crates/enforcer-lang-security/src/rules/spec.rs RuleSpec.suppressed_by_any_of; src/generic-scanner-shared.mjs's scanSecretLine SEC-2.11/.12/.14 && ! conditions; src/generic-common-line-rules.mjs's SEC-2.16/.17/.18 gitleaks/trufflehog && ! conditions

statement: Path-target rules (SEC-1.2 sensitive-files, SEC-2.19 SSH keys, SEC-2.20 mobile config) test the fixture's REPO-RELATIVE PATH itself, not its content — so the fixture FILE'S OWN BASENAME must literally match the forbidden pattern (e.g. exactly `.env`, `id_rsa`, `google-services.json`), not a descriptive slug like `fail.env` or `fail-ssh-key.txt`. A fixture named `fail.env` does NOT match `(^|/)\.env(\..+)?$` because the regex requires the segment to START with a dot, and `fail.env` starts with `fail`, not a dot.
why: This is easy to get backwards from the content-target rules' convention (where `fail.txt`/`pass.txt` slugs are fine because the MATCHER never inspects the filename) — a worker copying that convention for a path-target rule produces a fixture that silently never fires (DidNotFireOnFail), which only surfaces once `run_fixture_parity` is actually run, not at compile time.
howToApply: For any path-target Validator/RuleSpec (MatchTarget::Path in this crate's shape), put the fixture in a subdirectory and give the FILE ITSELF the exact forbidden basename (e.g. `fixtures/<slug>/fail/.env`, `fixtures/<slug>/fail/id_rsa`, `fixtures/<slug>/fail/google-services.json`), and pass that literal path string into run_fixture_parity — verified against `.env`/`.env.example` (dotfiles are NOT git-ignored by this repo's default .gitignore, confirmed via `git check-ignore`) and `id_rsa`/`google-services.json` fixtures in crates/enforcer-lang-security/fixtures/{sec-1-2,sec-2-19,sec-2-20}/.

evidence.ref: crates/enforcer-lang-security/fixtures/sec-1-2/fail/.env, fixtures/sec-2-19/fail/id_rsa, fixtures/sec-2-20/fail/google-services.json — all path-basename-exact fixtures required for their MatchTarget::Path specs to fire
